name: Locus of Control
one_line_summary: Rotter's dimension contrasting internal vs external attribution of control over events.
extended_summary: Locus of Control, developed by Julian Rotter and presented in his 1966 monograph 'Generalized Expectancies for Internal Versus External Control of Reinforcement', is the dimension along which individuals differ in attributing the causes of events in their lives to factors within themselves (internal locus) or to factors outside themselves such as luck, fate, or powerful others (external locus). Rotter's framework grew out of his broader social learning theory and is operationalized through the I-E Scale, a 29-item forced-choice instrument. Internal locus is typically associated with greater initiative, achievement motivation, problem-focused coping, and resistance to social influence; external locus is associated with greater learned helplessness, depression risk, and conformity. The construct has produced an enormous empirical literature in personality, clinical, and educational psychology, with subsequent extensions distinguishing health locus of control, work locus of control, and other domain-specific variants.
originators: Julian B. Rotter
year_or_decade: 1966 (foundational monograph)
core_components: Internal locus of control (events caused by own actions); External locus of control (events caused by luck, fate, powerful others); I-E Scale (Rotter's 29-item forced-choice instrument); Connection to social learning theory; Domain-specific variants (health LOC, work LOC, academic LOC); Continuity rather than discrete categories
primary_use_case: Personality and individual-difference research; clinical assessment and treatment planning; organizational psychology and work motivation research; health psychology (health locus of control); educational psychology (academic LOC); broad influence on understanding agency and self-direction.
common_criticisms: Treats locus as relatively stable trait when it has substantial situational variation; original I-E Scale criticized on factor-analytic grounds — the scale appears to measure several distinct constructs rather than a single dimension; cultural variation in attribution norms (collectivist vs individualist) makes cross-cultural comparison challenging; 'locus' framing oversimplifies attributions which can vary by domain, controllability, and stability dimensions (Weiner's attribution theory provides a more elaborated alternative); excessive internal locus can produce self-blame for genuinely external constraints; correlations with outcomes are typically modest.
primary_sources: Rotter, J.B. (1966). 'Generalized Expectancies for Internal Versus External Control of Reinforcement', Psychological Monographs
siblings: Self-Efficacy Theory; Learned Helplessness; Social Learning Theory

name: Learned Helplessness
one_line_summary: Seligman's account of passivity arising from repeated uncontrollable aversive events.
extended_summary: Learned Helplessness was identified by Martin Seligman and Steven Maier in animal-conditioning experiments at the University of Pennsylvania in 1967, in which dogs exposed to inescapable shocks subsequently failed to escape shock when escape became possible — having learned that their behavior could not affect outcomes. Seligman elaborated the construct into a model of human depression in Helplessness: On Depression, Development, and Death (1975), and Abramson, Seligman, and Teasdale's 1978 reformulation incorporated attributional dimensions (internal/external, stable/unstable, global/specific) to explain why some individuals exposed to uncontrollability develop helplessness while others do not. Hopelessness theory (Abramson, Metalsky, Alloy 1989) further elaborated this. Notably, Maier and Seligman's 2016 retrospective revised the 1967 interpretation: based on subsequent neuroscience, they argued the original finding was the opposite of what they had assumed — passivity is the default response to prolonged stress, and what is actually 'learned' is control rather than helplessness. The construct has been substantially influential in depression theory, motivation research, and the development of Seligman's Positive Psychology.
originators: Martin E.P. Seligman; Steven F. Maier; subsequent reformulation by Lyn Abramson, Lauren Alloy, Gerald Metalsky, John Teasdale
year_or_decade: 1967 (initial experiments); 1975 (Seligman book); 1978 (attributional reformulation); 2016 (Maier-Seligman revision)
core_components: Original triadic design (escapable shock / inescapable shock / no shock); Failure to escape after inescapable exposure; Three deficit components: motivational, cognitive, emotional; Attributional reformulation (internal/external, stable/unstable, global/specific); Hopelessness theory extension; 2016 Maier-Seligman revision (passivity as default; control is what is learned)
primary_use_case: Depression research and clinical theory; motivation and educational psychology (academic helplessness); workplace and burnout research; foundation for Seligman's subsequent Positive Psychology and learned-optimism interventions; framework underlying explanations of trauma response, abuse-relationship dynamics, and chronic illness coping.
common_criticisms: Animal-to-human generalization is contested; original 1967 interpretation was substantially revised by Maier and Seligman in 2016 based on neuroscience evidence; attributional reformulation has methodological challenges (attributional measures have weak psychometric properties); hopelessness depression as distinct subtype is empirically uneven; deterministic readings overstate continuity from learned helplessness in lab to clinical depression in life; clinical applications should be cautious about implying victims of uncontrollable circumstances have a 'helplessness disorder'.
primary_sources: Seligman, M.E.P. (1975). Helplessness: On Depression, Development, and Death; Abramson, L.Y., Seligman, M.E.P. & Teasdale, J.D. (1978). 'Learned Helplessness in Humans: Critique and Reformulation', Journal of Abnormal Psychology; Maier, S.F. & Seligman, M.E.P. (2016). 'Learned Helplessness at Fifty: Insights from Neuroscience', Psychological Review
siblings: Locus of Control; Self-Efficacy Theory; Cognitive Behavioral Therapy

name: Positive Psychology
one_line_summary: Seligman's flourishing framework: Positive emotion, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, Accomplishment.
extended_summary: Positive Psychology was launched as an organized scientific movement by Martin Seligman during his 1998 American Psychological Association presidency, with the explicit aim of redirecting psychological research and practice from its predominant focus on pathology toward scientific understanding of well-being, character strengths, and the conditions that produce human flourishing. Foundational figures alongside Seligman include Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (flow), Christopher Peterson (character strengths), Barbara Fredrickson (broaden-and-build), Ed Diener (subjective well-being), and Sonja Lyubomirsky (happiness interventions). The PERMA model, articulated in Seligman's Flourish (2011), identifies five elements of well-being: Positive emotion, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, and Accomplishment. Adjacent frameworks include the VIA Classification of 24 character strengths and Seligman's earlier authentic-happiness model. Positive Psychology has produced a substantial intervention literature and influenced education, workplace mental health, and therapy, though core claims have faced replication challenges in the broader social-psychology replication crisis.
originators: Martin E.P. Seligman; Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi; Christopher Peterson; Barbara Fredrickson; Ed Diener; Sonja Lyubomirsky
year_or_decade: 1998 (Seligman APA address); 2002 (Authentic Happiness book); 2011 (Flourish and PERMA)
core_components: PERMA: Positive emotion, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, Accomplishment; VIA Classification of 24 character strengths under 6 virtues; Subjective Well-Being (SWB) tradition (Diener); Flow as central to Engagement; Distinction between hedonic (pleasure) and eudaimonic (meaning) well-being; Positive interventions (gratitude practices, three good things, signature strengths use); Authentic happiness model (precursor)
primary_use_case: Foundation of well-being research and intervention; school-based positive education programs (Geelong Grammar, Penn Resilience); workplace well-being initiatives; clinical complement to traditional pathology-focused treatment; foundation for life and executive coaching; framework for thinking about flourishing in public-policy and organizational contexts.
common_criticisms: Several signature studies (some happiness interventions, certain positive-emotion findings) have struggled to replicate in the broader social-psychology replication crisis; critics including Barbara Held and Ronald Miller argue the movement undervalues the genuinely useful role of negative emotion and pathologizes appropriate distress; intervention effect sizes are typically modest and decay over time; cultural specificity of 'flourishing' frame raises cross-cultural concerns; commercial coaching and self-help adjacent to Positive Psychology often substantially overclaim what the science supports; military-focused applications (Comprehensive Soldier Fitness) have drawn ethical and efficacy critiques; PERMA's specific five-factor structure is one of several competing well-being frameworks (e.g., Ryff's six dimensions).
primary_sources: Seligman, M.E.P. (2002). Authentic Happiness; Seligman, M.E.P. (2011). Flourish: A Visionary New Understanding of Happiness and Well-being; Peterson, C. & Seligman, M.E.P. (2004). Character Strengths and Virtues
siblings: Flow Theory; Broaden-and-Build Theory; Self-Determination Theory

name: Flow Theory
one_line_summary: Csikszentmihalyi's optimal experience at the balance of challenge and skill.
extended_summary: Flow Theory was developed by Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi at the University of Chicago through interview-based research with artists, athletes, surgeons, chess players, and other domain experts beginning in the 1970s, presented in Beyond Boredom and Anxiety (1975) and the popular Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience (1990). Flow is the psychological state of complete immersion in an activity, characterized by intense concentration, merging of action and awareness, loss of self-consciousness, distortion of time, and intrinsically rewarding experience. The state arises when challenge level and skill level are both high and roughly matched — too much challenge produces anxiety, too much skill produces boredom. Csikszentmihalyi identified prerequisites including clear proximal goals, immediate feedback, and the perception that the task is doable. The Experience Sampling Method, in which participants are signaled at random intervals to report current activity and experience, was developed substantially to study flow empirically. The framework has influenced game design, education, sports psychology, work design, and Positive Psychology, and is among the most empirically supported well-being constructs.
originators: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi
year_or_decade: 1970s development; 1975 (Beyond Boredom and Anxiety); 1990 (Flow popular book)
core_components: Challenge-skill balance (both high); Clear proximal goals; Immediate feedback; Action-awareness merging; Concentration on task at hand; Loss of self-consciousness; Distortion of time perception; Autotelic (intrinsically rewarding) experience; Experience Sampling Method; Flow channel between anxiety and boredom
primary_use_case: Game and product design (engagement and immersion); educational design (matching challenge to skill); sports and performance psychology; work design and intrinsic motivation research; clinical applications including treatment of attention and motivational difficulties; Positive Psychology (a core construct in PERMA's Engagement element).
common_criticisms: Flow as measured by self-report retrospection is subject to memory and social-desirability biases; ESM method addresses some but not all measurement concerns; the optimal-challenge claim has substantial empirical support but the precise challenge-skill ratio for flow varies across individuals and domains; flow can occur in destructive activities (gambling, video gaming addiction, work to detriment of relationships) — the autotelic quality doesn't guarantee net well-being; cultural variation in flow experiences underexplored in early work; commercial gamification often invokes flow to legitimize engagement designs that are more accurately addiction-pattern engineering than genuine flow.
primary_sources: Csikszentmihalyi, M. (1975). Beyond Boredom and Anxiety; Csikszentmihalyi, M. (1990). Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience; Csikszentmihalyi, M. (1996). Creativity: Flow and the Psychology of Discovery and Invention
siblings: Positive Psychology; Broaden-and-Build Theory

name: Dual-Process Theory
one_line_summary: Two modes of cognition: fast intuitive and slow deliberative, popularized by Kahneman.
extended_summary: Dual-Process Theory holds that human cognition operates through two qualitatively distinct modes of processing: System 1 (or Type 1), which is fast, automatic, intuitive, associative, parallel, and effortless, generating impressions, intuitions, and rapid pattern recognition; and System 2 (or Type 2), which is slow, deliberate, effortful, sequential, rule-based, and resource-limited, supporting reflection, calculation, and deliberate reasoning. The framework synthesizes converging research lines including Stanovich and West's heuristic-vs-analytic distinction, Sloman's associative-vs-rule-based reasoning, Evans's heuristic-and-analytic theory, and Kahneman and Tversky's heuristics-and-biases program. Daniel Kahneman's popularization in Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011) brought the System 1/System 2 vocabulary to wide public audiences. The framework has broad influence in cognitive psychology, behavioral economics, judgment and decision-making research, and applied domains including clinical assessment and product design. Subsequent debate has questioned whether the two systems are genuinely distinct architectures or simply ends of continua, with current scholarly consensus favoring more nuanced multi-process models.
originators: Keith Stanovich; Richard West; Steven Sloman; Jonathan Evans; Daniel Kahneman (popularization)
year_or_decade: 1980s-1990s convergent development; 2011 (Kahneman Thinking, Fast and Slow popularization)
core_components: System 1 (fast, automatic, intuitive, associative, parallel, effortless); System 2 (slow, deliberate, effortful, sequential, rule-based, resource-limited); Default-interventionist architecture (System 1 generates default; System 2 monitors and intervenes); Cognitive load reduces System 2; Heuristics and biases as System 1 outputs; Cognitive reflection as System 2 marker (Frederick CRT); Subsequent multi-process refinements
primary_use_case: Foundation of cognitive psychology and judgment-and-decision-making research; underpins behavioral economics applications; framework for understanding cognitive bias, heuristics, and choice architecture; clinical assessment of automatic-vs-deliberate processes; influence on product design (defaults, friction); pedagogical framework for teaching critical thinking.
common_criticisms: System 1/System 2 as architectural distinction has been substantially critiqued — Evans and Stanovich's 2013 review argued for type-not-system framing; many candidate System 1/System 2 markers (speed, automaticity, effort) don't always align; some empirical findings cited by Kahneman (notably some priming effects in Thinking, Fast and Slow) have failed to replicate in the social-psychology replication crisis; binary framing oversimplifies the multiple processes likely involved; popular adoption tends to reify 'two systems' as if they were brain structures; alternative frameworks including evolutionary, embodied, and Bayesian accounts offer different organizing principles.
primary_sources: Stanovich, K.E. & West, R.F. (2000). 'Individual Differences in Reasoning: Implications for the Rationality Debate?', Behavioral and Brain Sciences; Kahneman, D. (2011). Thinking, Fast and Slow; Evans, J.S.B.T. & Stanovich, K.E. (2013). 'Dual-Process Theories of Higher Cognition: Advancing the Debate', Perspectives on Psychological Science
siblings: Heuristics and Biases Program; Cognitive Behavioral Therapy

name: Cognitive Dissonance Theory
one_line_summary: Festinger's account of discomfort from holding contradictory beliefs and motivated rationalization.
extended_summary: Cognitive Dissonance Theory was introduced by Leon Festinger in A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance (1957), holding that an individual experiencing inconsistency among cognitions (beliefs, attitudes, behaviors) feels psychological discomfort and is motivated to reduce that dissonance by changing one or more cognitions, adding consonant cognitions, or trivializing the dissonance. The theory's classic empirical demonstration is the Festinger and Carlsmith (1959) study in which participants paid $1 to lie about a boring task subsequently rated the task as more enjoyable than those paid $20 — explained as the smaller payment producing greater dissonance, which was reduced by attitude change. Subsequent extensions include Bem's self-perception theory (offering a parsimonious alternative for some cases), Aronson's self-consistency reformulation (dissonance arises particularly when self-concept is threatened), and Cooper and Fazio's new look (dissonance requires perceived personal responsibility for aversive consequences). The theory is among the most cited and most empirically productive in social psychology, with application to topics from attitude change to choice rationalization to belief perseverance.
originators: Leon Festinger
year_or_decade: 1957 (foundational book); 1959 (Festinger-Carlsmith $1/$20 study)
core_components: Cognitive elements (beliefs, attitudes, behaviors); Consonance and dissonance among cognitions; Motivation to reduce dissonance; Three reduction strategies (change cognition, add consonant cognition, trivialize dissonance); Magnitude of dissonance proportional to importance and number of dissonant cognitions; Subsequent reformulations (self-perception, self-consistency, new look)
primary_use_case: Foundation for understanding attitude change, belief perseverance, post-decision rationalization, and motivated reasoning; influence on persuasion theory, marketing, and political communication; clinical relevance for understanding self-deception and resistance to evidence; framework underlying many behavior-change interventions that work by inducing commitment-inconsistency dissonance.
common_criticisms: Self-perception theory (Bem) provides alternative explanation for many dissonance findings without invoking aversive arousal; methodological concerns about whether dissonance is genuinely physiological discomfort or post-hoc explanation; difficulty distinguishing dissonance from other affective and motivational states; some classic findings have struggled to replicate cleanly in modern studies; cross-cultural variation in dissonance effects (Heine, Kitayama, others) complicates universalist claims; the new-look reformulations narrowed the original theory's scope substantially; theory's flexibility in identifying which cognitions are 'dissonant' raises concerns about post-hoc explanation.
primary_sources: Festinger, L. (1957). A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance; Festinger, L. & Carlsmith, J.M. (1959). 'Cognitive Consequences of Forced Compliance', Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology; Cooper, J. (2007). Cognitive Dissonance: 50 Years of a Classic Theory
siblings: Heuristics and Biases Program; Dual-Process Theory

name: Theory of Planned Behavior
one_line_summary: Ajzen's model: intention shaped by attitudes, norms, and perceived control.
extended_summary: The Theory of Planned Behavior, developed by Icek Ajzen in 1985 and presented systematically in 'The Theory of Planned Behavior' (1991), extends his earlier Theory of Reasoned Action (with Martin Fishbein, 1975) by adding perceived behavioral control as a third determinant of behavioral intention. The model holds that intention to perform a specific behavior is shaped by three independent constructs: attitude toward the behavior (positive or negative evaluation), subjective norms (perceived social pressure from important others), and perceived behavioral control (perceived ease or difficulty of performing the behavior). Intention then predicts behavior, with perceived behavioral control sometimes also having direct effects when actual control is constrained. Each of the three predictors is theorized to derive from underlying beliefs (behavioral, normative, control beliefs), accessible through elicitation interviews. TPB is among the most empirically applied frameworks in health-behavior research, with extensive application to predicting and changing behaviors including diet, exercise, condom use, smoking, voting, and recycling.
originators: Icek Ajzen; Martin Fishbein (Theory of Reasoned Action precursor)
year_or_decade: 1975 (Theory of Reasoned Action); 1985 (Theory of Planned Behavior introduction); 1991 (canonical formulation)
core_components: Three intention predictors: Attitude toward the behavior, Subjective norms, Perceived behavioral control; Intention as proximal predictor of behavior; Behavioral, normative, and control beliefs as underlying foundations; Behavior-specific application; Direct path from PBC to behavior when actual control is constrained; Belief elicitation methodology
primary_use_case: Health behavior research and intervention design; public health campaigns; behavior-change program design across domains including pro-environmental behavior, financial behavior, organizational behavior; framework underlying many social marketing and behavioral-science applications; standard reference in Theory of Planned Behavior questionnaire development.
common_criticisms: Sniehotta, Presseau, and Araújo-Soares's 2014 'Time to Retire the Theory of Planned Behavior' argued the framework's predictive value is limited and adds little beyond simpler intention-behavior models; intention-behavior gap is substantial — TPB explains intention well but intention-to-action translation poorly; the three predictors often correlate substantially, raising questions about distinct contributions; doesn't well address habits, automaticity, or unconscious processes (which dual-process and habit-formation literatures emphasize); cross-cultural validity uneven; predictions for any specific behavior require extensive elicitation work that limits practical scalability; 'rational actor' framing limits applicability to impulsive or addictive behaviors.
primary_sources: Fishbein, M. & Ajzen, I. (1975). Belief, Attitude, Intention, and Behavior; Ajzen, I. (1991). 'The Theory of Planned Behavior', Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes; Sniehotta, F.F., Presseau, J. & Araújo-Soares, V. (2014). 'Time to retire the theory of planned behaviour', Health Psychology Review
siblings: Self-Efficacy Theory; Transtheoretical Model; Fogg Behavior Model

name: Transtheoretical Model
one_line_summary: Prochaska and DiClemente's stages: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance.
extended_summary: The Transtheoretical Model was developed by James Prochaska and Carlo DiClemente at the University of Rhode Island through comparative analysis of psychotherapy systems in the late 1970s, presented in The Transtheoretical Approach (1984), and substantially extended to behavior-change contexts in the 1990s. The framework proposes that change unfolds through five (later six) stages: Precontemplation (no intention to change in the foreseeable future, often unaware of the problem); Contemplation (aware of the problem, considering change but not committed); Preparation (intending to take action soon, often with small initial steps); Action (overt behavior change); Maintenance (sustained change for at least six months); and Termination (where the new behavior is fully integrated and relapse risk is minimal). The model also articulates ten processes of change, decisional balance (pros and cons of changing), and self-efficacy as components, with stage-matched interventions theorized to be more effective than stage-mismatched ones. TTM has been substantially applied to smoking cessation (its origin domain) and extended to many other health behaviors.
originators: James O. Prochaska; Carlo C. DiClemente
year_or_decade: Late 1970s development; 1984 (The Transtheoretical Approach); 1992 ('In Search of How People Change')
core_components: Five (or six) stages of change: Precontemplation, Contemplation, Preparation, Action, Maintenance, (Termination); Ten processes of change (consciousness raising, dramatic relief, self-reevaluation, environmental reevaluation, self-liberation, social liberation, counterconditioning, helping relationships, reinforcement management, stimulus control); Decisional balance (pros and cons); Self-efficacy; Stage-matched interventions hypothesis
primary_use_case: Smoking cessation programs (origin domain); health behavior change broadly (diet, exercise, alcohol, drug use); foundation for stage-matched intervention design; widely cited in health communication and motivational interviewing training; basis for many corporate wellness program designs.
common_criticisms: West's 2005 'Time for a change: putting the Transtheoretical (Stages of Change) Model to rest' argued the discrete stages are arbitrary and not empirically supported as distinct categories — proposed stage boundaries are based on time intervals rather than psychological discontinuities; stage-matched intervention superiority claim has not been consistently demonstrated in meta-analyses; cyclical/spiral structure (relapse to earlier stages) is more rule than exception, complicating stage-matched application; classification of individuals into stages is methodologically unstable; popular adoption substantially overclaims what evidence supports; doesn't well address structural barriers and social determinants of behavior change.
primary_sources: Prochaska, J.O. & DiClemente, C.C. (1984). The Transtheoretical Approach: Crossing Traditional Boundaries of Therapy; Prochaska, J.O., DiClemente, C.C. & Norcross, J.C. (1992). 'In Search of How People Change: Applications to Addictive Behaviors', American Psychologist; West, R. (2005). 'Time for a change: putting the Transtheoretical (Stages of Change) Model to rest', Addiction
siblings: Theory of Planned Behavior; Motivational Interviewing; Fogg Behavior Model

name: Motivational Interviewing
one_line_summary: Miller and Rollnick's collaborative method for evoking change talk and resolving ambivalence.
extended_summary: Motivational Interviewing was developed by William R. Miller in his work with problem drinkers in the early 1980s and substantially codified in Miller and Stephen Rollnick's Motivational Interviewing: Preparing People to Change Addictive Behavior (1991), with subsequent editions broadening application beyond addiction. MI is a person-centered, directive counseling style for evoking change through resolution of ambivalence — explicitly designed to address resistance and lack of engagement that confronted other counseling approaches. The method's spirit comprises Partnership, Acceptance, Compassion, and Evocation (PACE), and four central processes structure the conversation: Engaging, Focusing, Evoking, and Planning. Specific techniques include Open questions, Affirmations, Reflective listening, and Summarizing (OARS), eliciting and reinforcing change talk while rolling with resistance rather than confronting it. MI has accumulated substantial empirical support across substance use, health behavior, treatment adherence, and criminal justice domains, with effect sizes typically modest but consistent.
originators: William R. Miller; Stephen Rollnick
year_or_decade: 1980s development; 1991 (first edition); 2002 (second edition); 2013 (third edition)
core_components: Spirit (PACE: Partnership, Acceptance, Compassion, Evocation); Four processes (Engaging, Focusing, Evoking, Planning); OARS micro-skills (Open questions, Affirmations, Reflections, Summaries); Change talk vs sustain talk; DARN-CAT (Desire, Ability, Reasons, Need, Commitment, Activation, Taking steps); Rolling with resistance; Developing discrepancy; Person-centered foundation (Carl Rogers' influence)
primary_use_case: Addiction treatment (origin domain); health behavior change including weight management, smoking cessation, medication adherence; clinical intervention for treatment ambivalence; criminal justice and parole settings; healthcare communication training; integration with CBT and other evidence-based therapies; widespread use in primary care.
common_criticisms: Effect sizes meta-analytically modest and decay over follow-up; direct comparisons with structured CBT show inconsistent advantage; treatment fidelity is critical and often poor in non-research settings, with manualized application losing the spirit; commercialization through MI training and certification industry varies in quality; works less well with severe pathology requiring more directive intervention; less consistent evidence for non-addiction domains than for original substance-use applications; some 'MI' as practiced in the field is difficult to distinguish from generic supportive counseling.
primary_sources: Miller, W.R. & Rollnick, S. (1991, multiple editions). Motivational Interviewing: Helping People Change; Miller, W.R. & Rollnick, S. (2013). Motivational Interviewing: Helping People Change (3rd ed.)
siblings: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy; Transtheoretical Model; Self-Determination Theory

name: Trauma-Informed Care
one_line_summary: Approach assuming widespread trauma and prioritizing safety, choice, collaboration, empowerment.
extended_summary: Trauma-Informed Care is an organizational and clinical approach grounded in recognition of the high prevalence of trauma in clinical and community populations and its pervasive impact on functioning, brain development, and engagement with services. The framework was substantially shaped by the CDC-Kaiser Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACE) Study (Felitti et al., 1998), which documented strong dose-response relationships between childhood adversity and adult health and behavioral outcomes, and by SAMHSA's 2014 'Concept of Trauma and Guidance for a Trauma-Informed Approach', which articulated four assumptions (the four Rs: Realize, Recognize, Respond, Resist re-traumatization) and six key principles: Safety; Trustworthiness and Transparency; Peer Support; Collaboration and Mutuality; Empowerment, Voice, and Choice; and Cultural, Historical, and Gender Issues. TIC is implemented in healthcare, behavioral health, education, child welfare, and criminal justice as a system-level orientation rather than a specific therapy.
originators: Sandra Bloom (Sanctuary Model precursor); Maxine Harris and Roger Fallot (early framing); SAMHSA (2014 codification); Vincent Felitti and Robert Anda (ACE Study)
year_or_decade: 1990s emergence; 1998 (Felitti et al. ACE Study); 2001 (Harris & Fallot trauma-informed services); 2014 (SAMHSA codification)
core_components: Four Rs: Realize trauma's widespread impact; Recognize signs in clients, families, staff; Respond by integrating knowledge into practice; Resist re-traumatization; Six principles: Safety, Trustworthiness and Transparency, Peer Support, Collaboration and Mutuality, Empowerment-Voice-Choice, Cultural-Historical-Gender Issues; ACE Study foundation; System-level rather than therapy-specific orientation
primary_use_case: Healthcare and behavioral health settings; child welfare and juvenile justice; education (trauma-informed schools); homelessness services; criminal justice; refugee and immigration services; organizational change framework for service-delivery systems with trauma-exposed populations.
common_criticisms: Implementation quality varies widely — 'trauma-informed' has been adopted as a label without substantive practice change in many settings; the framework provides broad orientation rather than specific intervention specifications, leaving room for vague application; ACE score's deterministic interpretation has been challenged by Anda and Felitti themselves who caution against using it for individual prediction; potential for retraumatization through intrusive screening when implemented without clinical care; cultural and historical-trauma extensions are essential but unevenly addressed; tension between trauma-informed care and other clinical priorities (e.g., evidence-based trauma treatment) when implementations privilege awareness over treatment delivery.
primary_sources: SAMHSA (2014). SAMHSA's Concept of Trauma and Guidance for a Trauma-Informed Approach; Felitti, V.J. et al. (1998). 'Relationship of Childhood Abuse and Household Dysfunction to Many of the Leading Causes of Death in Adults: The ACE Study', American Journal of Preventive Medicine; Harris, M. & Fallot, R.D. (2001). Using Trauma Theory to Design Service Systems
siblings: Polyvagal Theory; Attachment Theory; Cognitive Behavioral Therapy

name: Job Demands-Resources Model
one_line_summary: Demerouti and Bakker's framework explaining burnout and engagement at work.
extended_summary: The Job Demands-Resources Model was introduced by Evangelia Demerouti, Arnold Bakker, Friedhelm Nachreiner, and Wilmar Schaufeli in 2001 ('The Job Demands-Resources Model of Burnout', Journal of Applied Psychology) as a parsimonious framework integrating prior work-stress models. It holds that all working conditions can be classified into two categories: Job Demands (physical, psychological, social, or organizational aspects requiring sustained effort and associated with physiological or psychological costs — e.g., workload, time pressure, emotional demands, role conflict) and Job Resources (aspects functional in achieving work goals, reducing demand cost, or stimulating growth — e.g., autonomy, feedback, social support, learning opportunities). The model's two parallel processes are an Energetic process (high demands → exhaustion → ill-health) and a Motivational process (high resources → engagement → positive outcomes), with resources buffering the impact of demands. Personal resources (self-efficacy, optimism, resilience) and job crafting were added in subsequent extensions. JD-R has accumulated substantial empirical support and is widely used in occupational health psychology and organizational practice.
originators: Evangelia Demerouti; Arnold B. Bakker; Friedhelm Nachreiner; Wilmar B. Schaufeli
year_or_decade: 2001 (foundational paper); 2007 (Bakker-Demerouti expanded framework); 2017 (revised model with personal resources, job crafting)
core_components: Job Demands (physical, psychological, social, organizational); Job Resources (autonomy, feedback, social support, learning opportunities); Two parallel processes: Energetic (demands → exhaustion → ill-health) and Motivational (resources → engagement → positive outcomes); Resources buffer demand impact; Personal Resources (self-efficacy, optimism, resilience); Job Crafting; Burnout (UWES) and Work Engagement (Utrecht Work Engagement Scale) measurement
primary_use_case: Occupational health psychology research; workplace burnout and engagement assessment; organizational interventions to reduce burnout and increase engagement; HR analytics and employee experience programs; foundation for many corporate wellbeing initiatives; integration with leadership development and job design programs.
common_criticisms: Demands-resources distinction can be context-dependent — same factor can function as either depending on perception (e.g., challenge demands vs hindrance demands); reliance on self-report measures vulnerable to common-method bias; interactional effects (resources moderating demand impact) inconsistently observed in meta-analyses; cross-cultural variation in what counts as resource or demand; the model has expanded over time to incorporate many constructs, raising parsimony concerns; lacks integration with structural and political dimensions of work (power, precarity); intervention research thinner than measurement research.
primary_sources: Demerouti, E., Bakker, A.B., Nachreiner, F. & Schaufeli, W.B. (2001). 'The Job Demands-Resources Model of Burnout', Journal of Applied Psychology; Bakker, A.B. & Demerouti, E. (2007). 'The Job Demands-Resources Model: State of the Art', Journal of Managerial Psychology; Bakker, A.B. & Demerouti, E. (2017). 'Job Demands-Resources Theory: Taking Stock and Looking Forward', Journal of Occupational Health Psychology
siblings: Conservation of Resources Theory; Self-Determination Theory

name: Conservation of Resources Theory
one_line_summary: Hobfoll's stress theory: people seek to acquire and protect valued resources.
extended_summary: Conservation of Resources Theory was developed by Stevan Hobfoll and presented in 'Conservation of Resources: A New Attempt at Conceptualizing Stress' (American Psychologist, 1989), proposing a resource-based account of psychological stress. The central tenet is that individuals strive to obtain, retain, protect, and foster the things they value (resources), and that psychological stress occurs when (1) resources are threatened with loss, (2) resources are actually lost, or (3) resources fail to be gained following significant resource investment. Resources are categorized into four types: objects (physical possessions), conditions (e.g., tenure, marital status), personal characteristics (skills, traits like self-efficacy), and energies (e.g., time, money, knowledge). Two key principles: resource loss is disproportionately more powerful than resource gain (asymmetry), and people must invest resources to protect against resource loss, recover from losses, and gain resources (loss spirals and gain spirals can result). COR has been widely applied to workplace stress and burnout research, often paired with or compared to the Job Demands-Resources Model.
originators: Stevan E. Hobfoll
year_or_decade: 1989 (foundational paper); 2001 ('The Influence of Culture, Community and the Nested-Self in the Stress Process')
core_components: Resource categories: Objects, Conditions, Personal characteristics, Energies; Stress occurs from: actual loss; threatened loss; failure to gain after investment; Asymmetry: loss more powerful than equivalent gain; Resource investment to protect/recover/gain; Loss spirals (resource depletion accelerates further loss); Gain spirals (resource accumulation enables further gain); Caravan resources (clusters travel together)
primary_use_case: Stress and burnout research, particularly in occupational health psychology; framework for understanding chronic stressor accumulation and recovery; basis for crisis-recovery interventions; integration with organizational and clinical research on resilience; complement or comparison with Job Demands-Resources Model; foundation for some trauma-recovery research.
common_criticisms: Resource categories can become so broad as to fit almost any factor as a 'resource', limiting falsifiability; the asymmetry principle (loss > gain) is not unique to COR (compare prospect theory's loss aversion); operationalization of resources varies widely across studies, complicating cumulative empirical work; Halbesleben et al. 2014 review noted measurement and definitional inconsistencies; substantial overlap with related stress theories raises questions about distinct contribution; less precise predictions than some alternatives (e.g., JD-R two-process model); cultural variability in what counts as a resource underexplored.
primary_sources: Hobfoll, S.E. (1989). 'Conservation of Resources: A New Attempt at Conceptualizing Stress', American Psychologist; Hobfoll, S.E. (1998). Stress, Culture, and Community; Halbesleben, J.R.B., Neveu, J.-P., Paustian-Underdahl, S.C. & Westman, M. (2014). 'Getting to the "COR": Understanding the Role of Resources in Conservation of Resources Theory', Journal of Management
siblings: Job Demands-Resources Model

name: Broaden-and-Build Theory
one_line_summary: Fredrickson's theory that positive emotions broaden thought-action repertoires.
extended_summary: Broaden-and-Build Theory was developed by Barbara Fredrickson at the University of Michigan and presented in 'What Good Are Positive Emotions?' (Review of General Psychology, 1998) and 'The Role of Positive Emotions in Positive Psychology' (American Psychologist, 2001). The theory proposes that whereas negative emotions narrow attention and the action repertoire to specific survival-relevant responses (fight, flee, withdraw — products of evolutionary pressure), positive emotions broaden the momentary thought-action repertoire (joy invites play, interest invites exploration, contentment invites integration), which over time builds enduring personal resources — physical, intellectual, social, and psychological — that enhance survival and flourishing. The theory's signature empirical claim is the upward spiral: positive emotions broaden cognition and behavior, which builds resources, which produce more positive-emotion-eliciting experiences. Fredrickson's 2005 specific 'positivity ratio' claim (3:1 positive-to-negative emotion required for flourishing) was substantially retracted following Brown, Sokal, and Friedman's 2013 critique that the underlying nonlinear-dynamics math was incorrect, but the broader broaden-and-build framework remains substantially supported empirically.
originators: Barbara L. Fredrickson
year_or_decade: 1998 (initial paper); 2001 (American Psychologist elaboration); 2009 (Positivity book); 2013 (positivity-ratio retraction)
core_components: Negative emotions narrow thought-action repertoire (evolutionary survival logic); Positive emotions broaden thought-action repertoire; Broadening over time builds personal resources (physical, intellectual, social, psychological); Upward spiral; Connection to attention research and cognitive-flexibility findings; Positivity-ratio claim (subsequently retracted on methodological grounds)
primary_use_case: Positive Psychology research and intervention design; emotion regulation research; workplace and team-effectiveness interventions; relationship and couples research; complement to negative-emotion-focused clinical research; framework underlying many gratitude and savoring practices.
common_criticisms: The 'positivity ratio' (3:1) claim was substantially retracted following Brown, Sokal, and Friedman's 2013 critique that the underlying nonlinear-dynamics math was incorrect — Fredrickson published a partial correction; subsequent meta-analyses of positive-emotion intervention effects show modest and decaying effects; popular adoption substantially overstates what evidence supports; broadening claim more robustly supported than building claim (which requires longitudinal evidence); cultural variation in positive-emotion experience and expression underweighted; risk of pathologizing necessary or appropriate negative emotion in popular adaptations.
primary_sources: Fredrickson, B.L. (1998). 'What Good Are Positive Emotions?', Review of General Psychology; Fredrickson, B.L. (2001). 'The Role of Positive Emotions in Positive Psychology', American Psychologist; Brown, N.J.L., Sokal, A.D. & Friedman, H.L. (2013). 'The Complex Dynamics of Wishful Thinking: The Critical Positivity Ratio', American Psychologist
siblings: Positive Psychology; Flow Theory

name: Karpman Drama Triangle
band_notes: Clinically useful schema; not empirically tested as a falsifiable theory.
one_line_summary: Three relational roles in conflict: Persecutor, Victim, Rescuer.
extended_summary: The Karpman Drama Triangle was introduced by Stephen Karpman in his 1968 paper 'Fairy Tales and Script Drama Analysis' (Transactional Analysis Bulletin) within the broader Transactional Analysis tradition. The framework identifies three interlocking psychological roles people unconsciously adopt in dysfunctional interpersonal dynamics: Persecutor (the blamer or aggressor — 'It's all your fault'); Victim (the helpless one — 'Poor me'); and Rescuer (the helper — 'Let me help you,' typically without solicitation and often perpetuating dependence). All three roles avoid genuine responsibility — Persecutor blames, Victim avoids agency, Rescuer's help maintains the Victim's victim position — and individuals frequently rotate among the roles within a single interaction. Acey Choy's 1990 'Winner's Triangle' and David Emerald's 2005 'TED Empowerment Dynamic' offer healthier role alternatives (Challenger, Vulnerable, Coach in Choy; Creator, Challenger, Coach in Emerald) for clinical and coaching application. The framework is widely used clinically and in coaching, particularly because it offers a memorable diagnostic structure for relational patterns.
originators: Stephen B. Karpman
year_or_decade: 1968 (Fairy Tales and Script Drama Analysis)
core_components: Three roles: Persecutor (blamer), Victim (helpless), Rescuer (unsolicited helper); Role rotation within interactions; All roles avoid genuine responsibility; Connection to Transactional Analysis games; Healthier alternatives: Choy's Winner's Triangle (Challenger, Vulnerable, Coach); Emerald's TED Empowerment Dynamic (Creator, Challenger, Coach); Diagnostic for codependent and conflict patterns
primary_use_case: Couples and family therapy; coaching for managing interpersonal patterns; workplace conflict-resolution training; clinical work with codependency, addiction-related dynamics, and abusive relationships; teaching tool in TA and broader counseling training; common framework in popular self-help and relationship literature.
common_criticisms: Not empirically tested as a falsifiable theory — primarily a clinical schema rather than a research-grounded model; categorization of any conflict can be made to fit the three roles, raising falsifiability concerns; oversimplifies complex dynamics that involve more than three roles or different configurations; commercial coaching adoption sometimes uses the triangle to label normal disagreement as 'drama'; can foster self-righteous spotting of others' roles rather than self-reflection; risks pathologizing legitimate distress as 'victim role'; doesn't address structural and contextual contributors to apparent role behavior.
primary_sources: Karpman, S. (1968). 'Fairy Tales and Script Drama Analysis', Transactional Analysis Bulletin; Karpman, S. (2014). A Game Free Life: The Definitive Book on the Drama Triangle and the Compassion Triangle
siblings: Transactional Analysis

name: Choice Theory
band_notes: Glasser's framework has practitioner adoption but limited rigorous empirical research.
one_line_summary: Glasser's framework of human behavior driven by five basic needs.
extended_summary: Choice Theory (originally Control Theory) and its therapeutic application Reality Therapy were developed by William Glasser, with Reality Therapy presented in his 1965 book of that name and Choice Theory codified in Choice Theory: A New Psychology of Personal Freedom (1998). Choice Theory holds that all behavior is purposeful and chosen (rather than caused by external events) in service of meeting five genetically-encoded basic needs: Survival (food, shelter, safety), Love and Belonging, Power (achievement, recognition), Freedom (autonomy), and Fun (enjoyment, learning). Each individual builds a 'quality world' of specific people, things, and ideals that meet their needs, and behavior is generated to close the gap between the quality world and current perception. Reality Therapy applies the framework clinically through the WDEP procedure (Wants, Doing, Evaluation, Planning) to help clients evaluate whether their current behavior is meeting needs and to plan more effective alternatives. The framework has been widely applied in education, addiction treatment, and counseling.
originators: William Glasser
year_or_decade: 1965 (Reality Therapy); 1998 (Choice Theory codification)
core_components: Five basic needs: Survival, Love and Belonging, Power, Freedom, Fun; All behavior as chosen and purposeful; Quality World (mental images of need-meeting people, things, ideals); Total behavior (acting, thinking, feeling, physiology); WDEP procedure (Wants, Doing, Evaluation, Planning); Reality Therapy as clinical application; Critique of external-control psychology
primary_use_case: Reality Therapy clinical application; education (Glasser Quality Schools); addiction treatment; school counseling; pastoral counseling; coaching; basis for Glasser's later 'lead-management' approach to organizational leadership.
common_criticisms: Empirical research on Reality Therapy outcomes is limited compared to evidence-based therapies; the five-needs taxonomy is asserted rather than empirically derived from independent factor-analytic work; 'all behavior is chosen' framing oversimplifies the substantial empirical evidence on automatic, habitual, and unconsciously-determined behavior; can foster harsh moralism (mental illness as choice) when applied beyond its appropriate scope; Glasser's broader 'mental health is about choice' rhetoric in his later work was contested and harmful when applied to severe mental illness; Reality Therapy's directive style is not a fit for all clinical populations; commercial William Glasser Institute training varies in rigor.
primary_sources: Glasser, W. (1965). Reality Therapy: A New Approach to Psychiatry; Glasser, W. (1998). Choice Theory: A New Psychology of Personal Freedom; Wubbolding, R.E. (2000). Reality Therapy for the 21st Century
siblings: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy; Self-Determination Theory

name: Gottman Sound Relationship House
one_line_summary: Empirically derived model of healthy couple relationships across nine levels.
extended_summary: The Sound Relationship House was developed by John and Julie Gottman through decades of observational research on married couples at the Gottman Institute and the University of Washington's 'Love Lab', presented in The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work (1999) and refined in subsequent works including The Marriage Clinic (1999). The framework synthesizes findings from longitudinal studies in which couples' interactions were coded second-by-second and physiological measurements taken, with subsequent marital outcomes tracked over years to identify behavioral and physiological predictors of stable, satisfying relationships versus dissolution. The 'house' metaphor organizes nine components: a foundation of Trust and Commitment, ascending floors of Build Love Maps, Share Fondness and Admiration, Turn Toward Bids, Positive Perspective, Manage Conflict, Make Life Dreams Come True, and Create Shared Meaning. Distinctive empirical contributions include the Four Horsemen (criticism, contempt, defensiveness, stonewalling) as predictors of dissolution, the 5:1 magic ratio of positive to negative interactions during conflict for stable relationships, and the importance of bid responsiveness to small attempts at connection.
originators: John M. Gottman; Julie Schwartz Gottman
year_or_decade: Decades of research from the 1970s onward; 1999 (Seven Principles popular synthesis)
core_components: Foundation: Trust and Commitment; Build Love Maps; Share Fondness and Admiration; Turn Toward (Bids and Responses); Positive Perspective; Manage Conflict; Make Life Dreams Come True; Create Shared Meaning; Four Horsemen (Criticism, Contempt, Defensiveness, Stonewalling); 5:1 positive-to-negative interaction ratio; Bids for connection; Antidote responses to each Horseman; Couples therapy method (Gottman Method Couples Therapy)
primary_use_case: Couples therapy and relationship counseling; premarital education programs; marital research and assessment (Gottman's Sound Relationship House Questionnaire); relationship education curricula; popular self-help; integration in some integrated behavioral couples therapy approaches.
common_criticisms: Some specific empirical claims (e.g., divorce-prediction accuracy of 90%+ from short observation) have been challenged on methodological grounds (Heyman & Slep critiques); reliance on Gottman Institute's commercial structure raises some independent-replication concerns; cross-cultural validity has not been thoroughly established — most foundational research is on US heterosexual couples; framework has expanded over time to incorporate many constructs without always-clear theoretical integration; Gottman's claims about same-sex couples drew on smaller samples than heterosexual research; popular adoption sometimes oversimplifies the framework; effect sizes for Gottman Method Couples Therapy comparable to but not clearly superior to Emotionally-Focused Therapy.
primary_sources: Gottman, J.M. (1999). The Marriage Clinic; Gottman, J.M. & Silver, N. (1999). The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work; Gottman, J.M. & Gottman, J.S. (2017). The Science of Couples and Family Therapy
siblings: Attachment Theory

name: Adlerian Individual Psychology
band_notes: Influential in counseling traditions; limited contemporary empirical research.
one_line_summary: Adler's framework emphasizing inferiority, social interest, and lifestyle.
extended_summary: Alfred Adler's Individual Psychology, developed after his 1911 break from Freud's psychoanalytic movement and presented in works including Understanding Human Nature (1927) and Social Interest: A Challenge to Mankind (1933), reframed psychoanalytic theory around social embeddedness, conscious goal-directedness, and the holistic indivisibility of the person. Central concepts include: feelings of inferiority as a universal developmental experience driving compensation and growth; the inferiority complex as pathological compensation; the superiority striving as healthy compensation aimed at competence and contribution; lifestyle (Lebensstil) as the unique pattern of beliefs, goals, and behaviors that emerges in early childhood and organizes adult life; social interest (Gemeinschaftsgefühl) as the criterion of mental health — the capacity for cooperative engagement with others and contribution to community welfare; and the encouraging vs discouraging stance in counseling and parenting. Adlerian thought has had substantial indirect influence (visible in CBT's emphasis on cognition, in humanistic psychology, in birth-order pop psychology, and recently in the resurgent self-help interest in Adler via Kishimi and Koga's The Courage to Be Disliked) though it has remained somewhat outside mainstream empirical psychology.
originators: Alfred Adler; subsequent figures including Rudolf Dreikurs, Heinz and Rowena Ansbacher, Don Dinkmeyer
year_or_decade: 1911 (break from Freud); 1927 (Understanding Human Nature); 1933 (Social Interest)
core_components: Feelings of inferiority and compensation; Inferiority complex (pathological); Superiority striving (healthy); Lifestyle / life style (Lebensstil) — unique organizing pattern of beliefs and goals; Social interest (Gemeinschaftsgefühl) as mental-health criterion; Birth order influences on personality; Family constellation; Encouraging counseling stance; Goal-directed view of behavior; Holism (indivisible person)
primary_use_case: Counseling and psychotherapy traditions emphasizing social embeddedness and goal-directedness; school and parent education (Dreikurs' Children: The Challenge); influence on humanistic and cognitive therapies; coaching and self-development; popular self-help via Kishimi and Koga's The Courage to Be Disliked; integration with positive-psychology and meaning-centered approaches.
common_criticisms: Limited contemporary peer-reviewed empirical research on Adlerian therapy outcomes compared to CBT-family approaches; birth-order claims have weak empirical support in modern research; some Adlerian concepts (lifestyle, social interest) are difficult to operationalize for measurement; framework often subsumed into other approaches without explicit acknowledgment; commercial training through Adlerian institutes varies in rigor; can become moralistic when 'social interest' is invoked normatively without engaging the framework's full analytical content; works less well as a discrete intervention package than as a conceptual orientation.
primary_sources: Adler, A. (1927). Understanding Human Nature; Adler, A. (1933). Social Interest: A Challenge to Mankind; Ansbacher, H.L. & Ansbacher, R.R. (1956). The Individual Psychology of Alfred Adler
siblings: Object Relations Theory; Self Psychology; Jungian Analytical Psychology

name: Object Relations Theory
band_notes: Influential in clinical psychoanalysis; not amenable to standard empirical validation.
one_line_summary: Psychoanalytic school focusing on internalized representations of self and others.
extended_summary: Object Relations Theory is the British psychoanalytic tradition that shifted Freudian psychoanalysis from drive-based motivation toward relationships as primary, with the 'object' referring to the other person (or part of the other person — partial object) as represented in the subject's internal world. Key figures include Melanie Klein (developing the framework from the 1920s with concepts of paranoid-schizoid and depressive positions, projective identification, and unconscious phantasy), Donald Winnicott (good-enough mother, holding environment, transitional objects, true self vs false self), W.R.D. Fairbairn (object-seeking rather than pleasure-seeking primary motivation), Wilfred Bion (containment and reverie, alpha and beta function), and John Bowlby (whose Attachment Theory developed alongside but in some tension with Object Relations). The framework analyzes psychopathology in terms of disturbed early relationships internalized as patterns shaping adult relating, with treatment proceeding through the therapeutic relationship as a corrective experience. It has been substantially influential in psychoanalytic and psychodynamic psychotherapy, infant observation, and clinical training, while sitting outside the standard empirical-validation paradigm of contemporary clinical-trial research.
originators: Melanie Klein; Donald Winnicott; W.R.D. Fairbairn; Wilfred Bion; Michael Balint; Otto Kernberg (American extension)
year_or_decade: 1920s onward through twentieth century; British Psycho-Analytical Society Independent and Klein groups
core_components: Object as the other or part of other in internal representation; Internal world of object relations; Klein's paranoid-schizoid and depressive positions; Projective identification; Winnicott's good-enough mother, holding environment, transitional object, true/false self; Fairbairn's object-seeking primary motivation; Bion's containment and alpha function; Therapeutic relationship as corrective experience; Distinction from drive-based Freudian theory
primary_use_case: Psychoanalytic and psychodynamic psychotherapy training and practice; infant observation and developmental research; clinical work with personality disorders, particularly Kernberg's Transference-Focused Psychotherapy for borderline; influence on attachment theory and relational psychoanalysis; foundation for some couples therapy approaches; clinical understanding of severe interpersonal pathology.
common_criticisms: Core constructs are not amenable to standard empirical validation paradigms — projective identification, unconscious phantasy, Klein's positions resist falsifiable test design; Klein's clinical conclusions about infant inner life have been challenged as projection from adult clinical material; long-term and intensive psychoanalytic treatment is expensive and inaccessible to most populations; outcome research on object relations therapies is limited and often methodologically weaker than CBT trials; theoretical proliferation across different schools (Klein, Winnicott, Fairbairn, Bion) creates heterogeneity in practice; training is long and expensive, limiting practitioner numbers; clinical insight runs deeper than testability, an asymmetry that has limited integration with mainstream clinical psychology.
primary_sources: Klein, M. (1932). The Psycho-Analysis of Children; Winnicott, D.W. (1965). The Maturational Processes and the Facilitating Environment; Fairbairn, W.R.D. (1952). Psychoanalytic Studies of the Personality; Bion, W.R. (1962). Learning from Experience
siblings: Self Psychology; Adlerian Individual Psychology; Attachment Theory

name: Self Psychology
band_notes: Influential in clinical psychoanalysis; not amenable to standard empirical validation.
one_line_summary: Kohut's psychoanalytic framework centered on selfobject experiences and narcissistic development.
extended_summary: Self Psychology was developed by Heinz Kohut at the Chicago Psychoanalytic Institute, with foundational works The Analysis of the Self (1971) and The Restoration of the Self (1977). Kohut began as a classical Freudian but his clinical work with narcissistic patients led him to a fundamental revision: the self, rather than drives, became the central organizing concept, and 'selfobjects' (the experience of others as performing self-regulating functions for the subject — mirroring, idealizing, twinship) the central developmental and clinical construct. Kohut argued that healthy selfhood develops through age-appropriate selfobject experiences (a parent's mirroring response to the child's display of vitality, an idealized parent providing strength and calm, twinship experiences of essential alikeness with another), and that pathology results from chronic empathic failures. Treatment proceeds through empathic immersion, the development and analysis of selfobject transferences, and 'transmuting internalization' as the patient progressively builds self-regulating capacities through repeated optimal frustrations within an empathic relationship. Self Psychology has been substantially influential in contemporary psychoanalytic practice, particularly with narcissistic and self-regulation difficulties.
originators: Heinz Kohut
year_or_decade: 1971 (The Analysis of the Self); 1977 (The Restoration of the Self); 1984 (How Does Analysis Cure?, posthumous)
core_components: Self as central organizing concept; Selfobjects (others experienced as performing self-regulating functions); Three selfobject transferences: Mirroring, Idealizing, Twinship; Empathic immersion as primary clinical method; Transmuting internalization through optimal frustration; Bipolar self (ambitions and ideals); Narcissistic line of development distinct from object-love line; Empathic failure as pathology source
primary_use_case: Psychoanalytic and psychodynamic psychotherapy, particularly with narcissistic personality disorder and self-regulation difficulties; clinical training emphasizing empathic stance; integration with relational and intersubjective psychoanalytic schools; influence on contemporary trauma-informed psychodynamic work; substantial influence on Schwartz's Internal Family Systems and on intersubjective psychoanalysis.
common_criticisms: Like Object Relations Theory, core constructs (selfobject experience, transmuting internalization) are not amenable to standard empirical validation; clinical evidence dominates over controlled outcome research; long and expensive training and treatment limit accessibility; theoretical claims about narcissistic development are difficult to test independently of clinical observation that is interpreted through the framework; Kohut's writing style is dense and his theoretical claims evolved during his career, creating interpretive variability; tradition has produced multiple post-Kohutian schools with internal disagreements; integration with empirical developmental research has been limited.
primary_sources: Kohut, H. (1971). The Analysis of the Self; Kohut, H. (1977). The Restoration of the Self; Kohut, H. (1984). How Does Analysis Cure? (posthumous)
siblings: Object Relations Theory; Adlerian Individual Psychology; Attachment Theory

name: Heuristics and Biases Program
one_line_summary: Kahneman and Tversky's research program cataloguing systematic deviations from rational judgment.
extended_summary: The Heuristics and Biases Program was launched by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky's collaboration beginning in 1969, with foundational papers including 'Belief in the Law of Small Numbers' (1971), 'Subjective Probability: A Judgment of Representativeness' (1972), and 'Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases' (1974). The program cataloged systematic deviations of human judgment from the predictions of normative probability theory and decision theory, identifying mental shortcuts (heuristics) that often produce useful judgments but that systematically fail in identifiable ways (biases). Three foundational heuristics were articulated: Availability (judging probability by ease of recall), Representativeness (judging category membership by similarity to category prototype), and Anchoring and Adjustment (estimates pulled toward initial reference points). Subsequent decades expanded the catalog substantially — confirmation bias, hindsight bias, framing effects, base-rate neglect, the conjunction fallacy, and dozens more. The program produced Prospect Theory (1979), influenced behavioral economics decisively, and earned Kahneman the 2002 Nobel Prize in Economics (Tversky having died in 1996).
originators: Daniel Kahneman; Amos Tversky
year_or_decade: 1969 onward; 1974 (canonical Science paper); 2002 Nobel (Kahneman); 2011 (Thinking, Fast and Slow popularization)
core_components: Availability heuristic (probability judgment by ease of recall); Representativeness heuristic (similarity to category prototype); Anchoring and adjustment; Many subsequent biases including confirmation, hindsight, framing, base-rate neglect, conjunction fallacy, planning fallacy, optimism bias; Methodology: comparison of human judgment to normative standards; Connection to Prospect Theory and Dual-Process Theory; Distinction between System 1 (heuristic) and System 2 (analytic) processing
primary_use_case: Foundation of behavioral economics; basis for judgment-and-decision-making research; debiasing interventions in clinical, financial, medical, and intelligence-analysis contexts; foundation for nudge and choice-architecture work; influence on product and policy design; basis for critical-thinking education.
common_criticisms: Replication crisis in social psychology has affected several specific findings cited prominently in Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow (notably some priming effects); Gigerenzer and the 'fast and frugal heuristics' school (ABC research group) argue that heuristics are often ecologically rational rather than systematically biased, and that comparing human judgment to normative probability theory is the wrong yardstick; debiasing interventions show modest and inconsistent effects; bias catalog has grown to a point that almost any judgment can be labeled some bias post-hoc; limited integration with neurobiological accounts of decision-making; cross-cultural variation in some biases is substantial.
primary_sources: Tversky, A. & Kahneman, D. (1974). 'Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases', Science; Kahneman, D., Slovic, P. & Tversky, A. (1982). Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases; Kahneman, D. (2011). Thinking, Fast and Slow
siblings: Dual-Process Theory; Cognitive Dissonance Theory; Behavioral Economics

name: Cognitive Reframing
one_line_summary: Deliberately reinterpreting an event to alter its emotional charge.
extended_summary: Cognitive Reframing is the deliberate practice of identifying and modifying the interpretation of an event, situation, or experience to alter its emotional and behavioral consequences. The technique is foundational across the cognitive-behavioral therapy family, descending from Albert Ellis's REBT disputation and Aaron Beck's cognitive restructuring, and is also employed in solution-focused therapy, family therapy (where reframing often addresses systemic patterns rather than individual cognition), and a wide range of coaching and self-development applications. The cognitive-emotion-behavior triangle from CBT provides the theoretical foundation: because emotions and behaviors are largely shaped by interpretations of events rather than events themselves, modifying interpretations modifies their downstream effects. Reframing techniques include identifying cognitive distortions (catastrophizing, all-or-nothing thinking, mind-reading, etc.), generating alternative interpretations, examining evidence for and against existing interpretations, and developing balanced perspectives. Distinct from positive thinking — reframing aims for accurate or useful rather than merely positive interpretation.
originators: Aaron T. Beck (cognitive restructuring); Albert Ellis (REBT disputation); systemic family therapy traditions (different reframe construct)
year_or_decade: 1960s-1970s codification within CBT family
core_components: Identification of automatic thoughts; Recognition of cognitive distortions; Generation of alternative interpretations; Examining evidence for and against; Behavioral experiments to test interpretations; Distinction between reframe (changing interpretation) and reappraisal (broader emotion regulation strategy); Distinction from positive thinking (accuracy, not positivity, is goal)
primary_use_case: Standard technique in CBT and CBT-family therapies for depression, anxiety, trauma, and many other conditions; coaching applications; emotion regulation training; resilience-building programs; self-help and journaling practices; integration with mindfulness practice (notice-then-reframe).
common_criticisms: Effective in well-bounded application but can become invalidating when used to dismiss legitimate distress responses to genuinely difficult circumstances; reframing requires capacity for cognitive flexibility that is reduced in severe depression and acute trauma; risk of becoming intellectualized rationalization that doesn't reach the emotional level; doesn't address structural and contextual contributors to distress; popular adaptations sometimes encourage 'just reframe it' superficiality that misses the careful interpretive work the technique requires; effectiveness depends on the skill with which alternative interpretations are generated.
primary_sources: Beck, A.T. (1976). Cognitive Therapy and the Emotional Disorders; Ellis, A. (1962). Reason and Emotion in Psychotherapy; Beck, J.S. (1995, multiple editions). Cognitive Behavior Therapy: Basics and Beyond
siblings: Thought Records; Behavioral Activation; Cognitive Behavioral Therapy

name: Thought Records
one_line_summary: CBT worksheet for identifying and challenging automatic thoughts.
extended_summary: Thought Records are the canonical worksheet-based technique of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy, used to systematically identify automatic thoughts and the situations and emotions associated with them, examine the evidence for and against those thoughts, generate balanced alternative thoughts, and re-rate emotions following cognitive work. Standard versions trace to Beck's cognitive therapy of the 1970s, with the seven-column Dysfunctional Thought Record (Situation, Emotion, Automatic Thought, Evidence For, Evidence Against, Balanced Alternative, Re-rated Emotion) being the most familiar format. Greenberger and Padesky's Mind Over Mood (1995, 2nd ed. 2015) provides the most widely-used self-help adaptation. Thought records operate as the operational form of cognitive restructuring — making the typically fast and implicit cognitive-emotion-behavior chain explicit and workable. They are used both in therapy sessions and as homework between sessions, with consistent use being one of the strongest predictors of CBT outcome.
originators: Aaron T. Beck (cognitive therapy origin); Christine Padesky and Dennis Greenberger (Mind Over Mood popularization)
year_or_decade: 1970s development within Beck's cognitive therapy; 1995 (Mind Over Mood)
core_components: Standard seven columns: Situation; Emotion (rated 0-100); Automatic Thought (rated for belief 0-100); Evidence For; Evidence Against; Balanced Alternative Thought; Re-rated Emotion (and re-rated belief in balanced thought); Variations: simpler ABC format; mood-ladder version; Use as homework between sessions; Pairing with cognitive distortion identification (catastrophizing, mind-reading, etc.)
primary_use_case: Core CBT homework tool for depression, anxiety disorders, and many other conditions; widely used in self-directed cognitive-behavioral interventions; component of clinical training in cognitive therapy; integration with apps and digital CBT platforms (MoodKit, Sanvello, others); foundation for related techniques including thought experiments and behavioral experiments.
common_criticisms: Worksheet format can feel mechanical and artificial; effectiveness depends on therapist skill in coaching the technique and on client follow-through, which is often poor; can encourage intellectualization without reaching emotional change; less suited to highly somatic or affective presentations; manualized administration risks losing the Socratic-collaborative spirit Beck emphasized; some clients experience the technique as invalidating; popular adoption sometimes simplifies to 'reframe' without the systematic evidence-examination that distinguishes the technique from generic positive thinking.
primary_sources: Beck, A.T., Rush, A.J., Shaw, B.F. & Emery, G. (1979). Cognitive Therapy of Depression; Greenberger, D. & Padesky, C.A. (1995, 2015). Mind Over Mood
siblings: Cognitive Reframing; Behavioral Activation; Cognitive Behavioral Therapy

name: Behavioral Activation
one_line_summary: Increasing engagement with rewarding activities to interrupt depressive cycles.
extended_summary: Behavioral Activation is a structured intervention for depression that targets the depressive cycle of withdrawal, decreased reward, and worsening mood by systematically increasing engagement with activities that provide pleasure (positive reinforcement) and mastery (competence-based reward). It descends from Charles Ferster's 1973 functional analysis of depression as reduced positive reinforcement, was operationalized in the behavior therapy of Lewinsohn (1974, depression as low rate of response-contingent positive reinforcement), and was rediscovered as a distinct treatment when Jacobson, Dobson, and colleagues' 1996 component analysis of cognitive therapy for depression found that the behavioral activation component alone produced equivalent outcomes to full CBT. Subsequent work by Martell, Addis, Jacobson, Dimidjian, and others developed behavioral activation as a standalone treatment with substantial empirical support — its 2006 trial showed it equivalent to antidepressant medication and superior to cognitive therapy for severe depression. The technique uses activity monitoring, value clarification, scheduling, and graded task assignment to increase contact with positive reinforcers.
originators: Charles B. Ferster (functional analysis); Peter Lewinsohn (behavioral approach to depression); Neil Jacobson, Christopher Martell, Sona Dimidjian (modern BA)
year_or_decade: 1973 (Ferster); 1974 (Lewinsohn); 1996 (Jacobson component analysis); 2001 (Martell, Addis & Jacobson, Depression in Context)
core_components: Activity monitoring (tracking activities and associated mood); Activity scheduling (planning specific positive activities); Value clarification (linking activities to what matters); Graded task assignment (breaking activities into manageable steps); Functional analysis (when, where, and why depressive avoidance occurs); Mastery and pleasure ratings; Distinction from CBT (no required cognitive intervention); Behavioral Activation Treatment for Depression (BATD) protocol
primary_use_case: First-line treatment for major depression, particularly severe depression where it has shown advantage over cognitive therapy alone; primary care and brief-treatment contexts where its lower complexity than full CBT enables broader delivery; treatment of comorbid depression in chronic illness; integration in CBT and as standalone in collaborative care models; extension to depression-related conditions including bereavement and adjustment.
common_criticisms: Less elaborated than full CBT, which limits applicability when cognitive symptoms are central; doesn't address rumination as directly as cognitive techniques; requires patient capacity for activity engagement that severe depression may compromise; activity scheduling can become mechanical without the values-clarification component; cultural variation in what counts as positive reinforcement underexplored; dismantling component analyses don't always replicate Jacobson 1996 findings in mixed samples; ongoing debate about whether BA's mechanism is positive reinforcement, avoidance reduction, or behavioral exposure.
primary_sources: Lewinsohn, P.M. (1974). 'A behavioral approach to depression', in Friedman & Katz (eds.) The Psychology of Depression; Jacobson, N.S. et al. (1996). 'A Component Analysis of Cognitive-Behavioral Treatment for Depression', Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology; Martell, C.R., Addis, M.E. & Jacobson, N.S. (2001). Depression in Context; Dimidjian, S. et al. (2006). 'Randomized Trial of Behavioral Activation, Cognitive Therapy, and Antidepressant Medication', Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
siblings: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy; Cognitive Reframing; Thought Records

name: Mindfulness Practice
band_notes: Originally Buddhist contemplative practice; now substantial empirical base in clinical contexts (MBSR, MBCT).
one_line_summary: Sustained non-judgmental attention to present experience.
extended_summary: Mindfulness Practice in its contemporary clinical form is the systematic cultivation of present-moment, non-judgmental, accepting awareness of experience — body sensations, breath, thoughts, emotions, and sensory input — as it arises and passes. The roots are in Buddhist contemplative traditions, particularly the satipaṭṭhāna (foundations of mindfulness) teachings of Theravada Buddhism and the analogous practices in Mahayana and Vajrayana traditions. The clinical translation began with Jon Kabat-Zinn's development of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) at the University of Massachusetts Medical Center in 1979, deliberately secularized for medical settings while preserving the contemplative substance. Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT, Segal-Williams-Teasdale 2002) extended the approach for depression relapse prevention, with NHS recommendation for recurrent depression. Contemporary clinical research includes thousands of trials with mostly favorable but heterogeneous results, and MBSR/MBCT have substantial evidence for chronic pain, recurrent depression, anxiety, and stress, with smaller and more mixed evidence for many secondary applications.
originators: Buddhist contemplative traditions (satipaṭṭhāna); Jon Kabat-Zinn (clinical translation, MBSR); Zindel Segal, Mark Williams, John Teasdale (MBCT)
year_or_decade: Buddhist roots ~5th century BCE onward; 1979 (Kabat-Zinn MBSR); 2002 (MBCT)
