core_components: Present-moment awareness; Non-judgmental observation; Body scan; Sitting meditation with breath as primary anchor; Mindful movement; Informal mindfulness in daily activities; Distinction from concentration practice (focus on single object); Integration with cognitive techniques in MBCT; Eight-week structured course format (MBSR, MBCT)
primary_use_case: Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) for chronic pain, stress, anxiety; Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT) for depression relapse prevention; component in Dialectical Behavior Therapy and Acceptance and Commitment Therapy; workplace and organizational wellness programs; integration with sport and performance psychology; underpinning of broader contemplative neuroscience research.
common_criticisms: Many secondary popular and workplace applications outpace the empirical evidence base; meta-analyses show modest effect sizes that tend to decay at follow-up; secularization for clinical use has been argued to strip mindfulness of the ethical and contemplative context that gave it depth ('McMindfulness' critique); decontextualized practice can produce adverse effects (anxiety, depersonalization, traumatic memory surfacing) that early enthusiasm did not adequately address — research on adverse effects has only matured in the past decade; commercial training varies widely in quality; cultural-appropriation concerns when Buddhist sources are unacknowledged; effectiveness may depend on substantial practice doses that many programs don't achieve.
primary_sources: Kabat-Zinn, J. (1990). Full Catastrophe Living; Segal, Z.V., Williams, J.M.G. & Teasdale, J.D. (2002). Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy for Depression; Bishop, S.R. et al. (2004). 'Mindfulness: A Proposed Operational Definition', Clinical Psychology: Science and Practice
siblings: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy; Dialectical Behavior Therapy

name: Box Breathing
one_line_summary: Inhale, hold, exhale, hold for equal counts to regulate the nervous system.
extended_summary: Box Breathing is a structured breathwork technique in which inhalation, breath-hold, exhalation, and second breath-hold are each performed for equal counts (commonly four seconds), forming the four 'sides' of the metaphorical box. The practice is rooted in pranayama traditions of yoga (with similarities to sama vritti and other equal-ratio breathing) and has been substantially popularized in Western contexts by US Navy SEAL Mark Divine in the 2010s and through subsequent military, performance, and self-help applications. The proposed mechanism is downregulation of sympathetic nervous system activation through the parasympathetic effects of slowed breathing, breath-holds, and the cognitive focus required to maintain the count — producing reduced heart rate, lowered cortisol, and subjective calming. Empirical evidence specifically for box breathing as a discrete technique is limited, but slow-breathing interventions broadly have a substantial evidence base for acute stress reduction and improved heart-rate variability, and the simplicity and accessibility of the technique have made it widely adopted.
originators: Pranayama yoga traditions (foundational); Mark Divine (Western popularization through SEAL training and Unbeatable Mind)
year_or_decade: Yoga roots ancient; 2010s Western popularization
core_components: Four phases of equal duration: Inhale, Hold (full lungs), Exhale, Hold (empty lungs); Standard four-second per phase (4-4-4-4); Variants with longer counts for advanced practice (5-5-5-5, 6-6-6-6); Nasal breathing typically; Repetitions of 4-10 cycles or sustained practice; Connection to broader pranayama and breathwork practices; Mechanism: sympathetic-to-parasympathetic shift
primary_use_case: Acute stress and anxiety regulation; pre-performance preparation in athletes, military, first responders, public speakers; sleep onset; integration with mindfulness practice; widely taught in trauma-informed and somatic work; foundational technique in many self-regulation and resilience training programs.
common_criticisms: Limited empirical research on box breathing specifically as distinguished from broader slow-breathing literature; mechanism claims often overstated relative to evidence; popular adoption sometimes presents the technique as a complete solution to chronic stress when it is principally an acute regulation tool; commercial and military marketing can overstate efficacy; breath-holds are contraindicated for some populations (pregnancy, hypertension, panic disorder); cultural-appropriation concerns when yoga sources are unacknowledged; works less well during acute panic when capacity to follow instructions is compromised.
primary_sources: Divine, M. (2014). The Way of the SEAL; broader literature on slow-paced breathing and HRV including Russo, M.A., Santarelli, D.M. & O'Rourke, D. (2017). 'The physiological effects of slow breathing in the healthy human', Breathe
siblings: Mindfulness Practice
